theory.intro: $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ says $X$ is normal with mean $\mu$ and **variance** $\sigma^{2}$, the square of the standard deviation. The **standard normal distribution** is $Z\sim N(0,1)$, the one curve with mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$.
facts: In $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ the second number is the variance, so the standard deviation is its square root.
$X\sim N(70,25)$ and $X\sim N(70,5^{2})$ describe the same variable, with mean $70$ and standard deviation $5$.
A distribution is standard normal only when both $\mu=0$ and $\sigma=1$; any other pair is non-standard.
Standardising uses $Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$, which subtracts the mean and then divides by the standard deviation.
Every normal variable standardises to the same curve, so one table of $z$ values serves all of them.
A $z$ value counts standard deviations, so it has no units even when $X$ is measured in grams or hours.
The score $x=\mu+\sigma$ always maps to $z=1$, whatever the mean and standard deviation happen to be.
steps: Read the first number in $N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ as the mean
Read the second number as the variance $\sigma^{2}$
Take the square root of the variance to get the standard deviation

foundation.question_text:
$X\sim N(70,25)$.
State the mean and the standard deviation of $X$.

$X\sim N(268,9^{2})$.
State the mean and the standard deviation of $X$.
foundation.solution_text:
The variance is already written as a square, so the standard deviation can be read straight off.
$\mu=268$
$\sigma^{2}=9^{2}$
$\sigma$
$=9$

foundation.question_text:
The volume of juice in a carton is normally distributed with mean $12.5$ mL above the label and standard deviation $0.4$ mL.
Write this using $N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ notation, with $X$ the excess volume in mL.
foundation.solution_text:
The second entry is the variance, so square the standard deviation.
$\sigma^{2}$
$=0.4^{2}$
$=0.16$
$X\sim N(12.5,0.16)$

foundation.question_text:
A normal random variable $W$ has mean $150$ and standard deviation $20$.
Write this using $N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ notation.

$X\sim N(0,4)$.
Explain whether $X$ has the standard normal distribution.
foundation.solution_text:
$\sigma$
$=\sqrt{4}$
$=2$
The mean is $0$, but the standard deviation is $2$ rather than $1$.
No, $X$ is not standard normal.

foundation.question_text:
$Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $W\sim N(1,1)$.
Explain which of these, if either, is standard normal.
foundation.solution_text:
$Z$ has mean $0$ and variance $1$, so its standard deviation is $1$ as well.
$W$ has standard deviation $1$, but its mean is $1$ rather than $0$.
Only $Z$ is standard normal.

foundation.question_text:
$X\sim N(50,64)$.
Write $P(X<66)$ as a probability about the standard normal variable $Z$.

$X\sim N(84,36)$.
State the mean and the standard deviation of $Z=\frac{X-84}{6}$.
foundation.solution_text:
$\sigma$
$=\sqrt{36}$
$=6$
Subtracting $84$ moves the centre of the distribution to $0$, and dividing by $6$ shrinks the spread by a factor of $6$.
The mean of $Z$ is $0$ and its standard deviation is $1$.

development.question_text:
$X\sim N(4.2,2.25)$.
State the mean and the standard deviation of $X$.

$X\sim N(120,225)$.
Write $P(X>96)$ as a probability about the standard normal variable $Z$.

$X\sim N(60,16)$ and $Y\sim N(500,100)$.
Show that $P(X<68)$ and $P(Y<520)$ are equal.
development.solution_text:
For $X$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{16}=4$.
$z$
$=\frac{68-60}{4}$
$=2$
For $Y$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{100}=10$.
$z$
$=\frac{520-500}{10}$
$=2$
Both scores standardise to $z=2$, so both probabilities equal $P(Z<2)$.

development.question_text:
A bottling machine fills bottles to a mean of $750$ mL with a standard deviation of $2.5$ mL.
Write the volume $V$ using $N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ notation.
Explain why the variable $Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$ always has mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$, whatever $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are.
development.solution_text:
Subtracting $\mu$ from every score shifts the whole distribution left by $\mu$, so the centre lands on $0$ and the spread is unchanged.
Dividing every shifted score by $\sigma$ shrinks every distance from the centre by a factor of $\sigma$, so a distance of one standard deviation becomes a distance of $1$.
The centre is therefore at $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$.

development.question_text:
Which of $N(0,1)$, $N(0,1^{2})$, $N(1,1)$ and $N(0,2)$ are standard normal distributions?
Explain.
development.solution_text:
$N(0,1)$ and $N(0,1^{2})$ are two ways of writing the same thing, since $1^{2}=1$, and both have mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$.
$N(1,1)$ has standard deviation $1$ but mean $1$.
$N(0,2)$ has mean $0$ but standard deviation $\sqrt{2}$.
Only $N(0,1)$ and $N(0,1^{2})$ are standard normal.

development.question_text:
$X\sim N(30,49)$ and $P(X<c)=P(Z<-2)$, where $Z$ is standard normal.
Find $c$.

mastery.question_text:
$X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$.
The score $x=43$ standardises to $z=1.5$ and the score $x=31$ standardises to $z=-0.5$.
Find $\mu$ and $\sigma$.
mastery.solution_text:
$43=\mu+1.5\sigma$
$31=\mu-0.5\sigma$
Subtracting the second equation from the first removes $\mu$.
$12=2\sigma$
$\sigma=6$
$\mu$
$=31+0.5\times 6$
$=34$

mastery.question_text:
$X\sim N(160,\sigma^{2})$, and the score $x=172$ standardises to $z=0.8$.
Find $\sigma^{2}$ and write the distribution in full $N(\mu,\sigma^{2})$ notation.

$X\sim N(25,9)$ and $Y\sim N(25,36)$.
A score of $31$ is recorded on each scale.
Explain which score is the more extreme.
mastery.solution_text:
For $X$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{9}=3$.
$z$
$=\frac{31-25}{3}$
$=2$
For $Y$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{36}=6$.
$z$
$=\frac{31-25}{6}$
$=1$
Both scores map onto the same standard normal curve, and $31$ sits two standard deviations out on the $X$ scale but only one on the $Y$ scale.
The score of $31$ on the $X$ scale is the more extreme.
